subject: ela
skillName: Identify different story points of view

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

Amara loved the snow. She ran to the window and said, "Snow day!" Her dad sighed and said, "That means I have to shovel the driveway again."

How does Amara feel about the snow?
items.answer: Amara feels excited and happy about the snow. She is looking forward to a snow day.

steps: Amara says 'Snow day!' with excitement — this shows she is happy.
Her reaction is positive: she runs to the window.
Her point of view is that snow is fun and exciting.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

The class pet, a turtle named Shell, barely moved all day. Marcus said, "I think he's bored." Sofia watched closely and said, "I think he's happy. Turtles are slow — that's just how they are."

What is Marcus's point of view about Shell?
items.answer: Marcus thinks Shell is bored because the turtle is not moving much. He believes the turtle's stillness is a sign of unhappiness.

steps: Marcus says 'I think he's bored' — he interprets the turtle's stillness as a negative feeling.
His point of view is that Shell needs more activity or stimulation.
This is the literal identification of his stated point of view.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

Leo and his sister Bea both saw the same large dog on the walk home. Leo said, "Can we pet him?" Bea stepped behind Leo and whispered, "Please keep walking."

How do Leo and Bea feel differently about the dog?
items.answer: Leo feels excited and wants to interact with the dog. Bea feels scared and wants to move away from it. The same dog makes one sibling curious and the other frightened.

steps: Leo's point of view: He wants to pet the dog — he sees it as friendly and interesting.
Bea's point of view: She hides behind Leo and wants to leave — she is afraid of the dog.
Same dog, opposite emotional reactions.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

The town added a new skate park. Twelve-year-old Dani was thrilled. "We've been asking for this for years!" Mrs. Patel, who lived next to the park, shook her head. "It will be noisy all afternoon and into the evening."

Compare Dani's and Mrs. Patel's points of view about the skate park. Use evidence from the story to explain how each character feels and why.
items.answer: Dani is thrilled because the skate park is something young people in the community had been requesting for a long time. She feels heard and excited. Mrs. Patel is unhappy because the park will bring noise right next to her home, affecting her peace. The evidence for Dani is 'We've been asking for this for years!' showing her sense of victory. The evidence for Mrs. Patel is 'noisy all afternoon and into the evening' showing her concern about the disruption. Same park, but Dani gains something and Mrs. Patel loses something.

steps: Dani's evidence: 'We've been asking for this for years!' — she sees it as a community achievement.
Dani's point of view: The park is a long-awaited win for young people.
Mrs. Patel's evidence: 'It will be noisy all afternoon and into the evening' — she sees it as a source of disruption.
Mrs. Patel's point of view: The park will hurt the quality of life near her home.
Both see the same park: one as a gain, one as a loss.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

Nadia's class was doing group projects. Their teacher, Mr. James, assigned the groups instead of letting students pick. Nadia said, "I was hoping to work with my friends." Her classmate Tomás said, "Good — now I can work with people I don't always talk to."

How do Nadia and Tomás feel differently about assigned groups? Use specific evidence from the story to support your answer.
items.answer: Nadia is disappointed because she wanted to work with her existing friends. The evidence is 'I was hoping to work with my friends,' which shows she values familiar social connections. Tomás is happy because he sees assigned groups as an opportunity to connect with people he does not usually talk to. The evidence is his comment about working with new people. The same policy is limiting for Nadia and exciting for Tomás.

steps: Nadia's evidence: 'I was hoping to work with my friends' — she prefers comfort and familiar relationships.
Nadia's point of view: Assigned groups take away the social connection she values.
Tomás's evidence: 'Now I can work with people I don't always talk to' — he sees opportunity for growth.
Tomás's point of view: Assigned groups open a door to new relationships.
Same policy = restriction for Nadia, opportunity for Tomás.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

Omar worked very hard on a drawing of a dragon for the class art show. His teacher said, "Wonderful detail on the wings." His younger sister looked at it and said, "The feet look funny."

How does Omar's teacher's point of view differ from his sister's? Use details from the story to explain both views.
items.answer: Omar's teacher focuses on the positive: she notices the detailed wings and praises them. Her point of view is encouraging and focused on craft. His younger sister points out a flaw: the feet look funny to her. Her point of view is more literal and critical. Both are looking at the same drawing, but the teacher sees the skill while the sister sees an imperfection. Their different ages and purposes shape what each one notices.

steps: Teacher's evidence: 'Wonderful detail on the wings' — she focuses on a strength.
Teacher's point of view: The drawing shows impressive artistic skill.
Sister's evidence: 'The feet look funny' — she notices what does not look right to her.
Sister's point of view: The drawing has something that looks off.
Teacher evaluates with encouragement; sister reacts with honest (and blunt) observation.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

Amara's family came from a country where water was scarce. When she moved to the United States, she was amazed that people left faucets running while brushing their teeth. She said something to her friend Kenji, who shrugged. "It's just water. There's plenty."

Explain why Amara and Kenji see the same act of leaving a faucet running so differently. What does each character's background contribute to their point of view?
items.answer: Amara grew up in a place where water was scarce, so she knows from personal experience how precious water is. To her, leaving a faucet running is wasteful and hard to watch. Kenji has grown up somewhere where water seems unlimited, so he has no experience of scarcity. He cannot imagine why it would be a problem. Their different backgrounds create completely different understandings of the same act. Amara's point of view is shaped by lived experience of shortage; Kenji's is shaped by never having lacked for water. Same faucet, same amount of water, but one character knows its value in a way the other has never had to learn.

steps: Amara's background: She grew up where water was scarce — she has lived through shortage.
Amara's point of view: Leaving a faucet running is wasteful and upsetting because water is precious.
Kenji's background: He has always had access to plentiful water and has never experienced shortage.
Kenji's point of view: 'There's plenty' — he genuinely cannot see the problem.
Why they differ: Amara knows from experience what water scarcity feels like; Kenji has never had to think about it.
Same faucet = a sign of waste for one; a non-issue for the other, based entirely on lived background.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

Sofia's class voted on whether to get a class pet. Most students voted yes. Sofia voted no but did not say why out loud. She thought, 'What if nobody remembers to feed it over break? What if it gets sick? What if it dies and everyone is sad?'

Explain Sofia's point of view and why it is different from most of her classmates'. What does her way of thinking reveal about her personality and how it shapes her point of view?
items.answer: Most of Sofia's classmates are excited about having a class pet and vote yes, focusing on how fun it would be. Sofia votes no because she is worried about what could go wrong: who will care for it during breaks, what happens if it gets sick or dies. Her point of view is shaped by her personality: she is a worrier who thinks ahead and considers consequences others have not thought about. While her classmates look at the best possible outcome, Sofia looks at the risk. Her point of view is not wrong, just different. It reveals a cautious, caring, and forward-thinking way of seeing the world.

steps: Classmates' point of view: A class pet sounds exciting and fun — they vote yes without apparent concern.
Sofia's point of view: A class pet comes with serious responsibilities and risks — she votes no.
Evidence of Sofia's thinking: She worries about feeding during breaks, illness, and death — she anticipates problems others ignore.
What this reveals about Sofia: She is cautious, empathetic, and thinks carefully about consequences.
Why their views differ: Most classmates think about the reward (fun); Sofia thinks about the risk (suffering).
Same idea, but viewed through the lens of optimism vs. careful concern.
